“I SERVED 14 YEARS. I GOT A PLAQUE WITH MY NAME MISSPELLED, AND A 15-YEAR PAYMENT PLAN.” — SEAL Team 6 Operator Matt Bissonnette on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most explosive interviews in the history of The Shawn Ryan Show (Episode #252), former DEVGRU assaulter Matt Bissonnette—who authored No Easy Day under the pen name "Mark Owen"—broke his 12-year silence on the raid that killed Osama bin Laden and the federal government's relentless legal retaliation against him.

In his own words:

“I’ve been fighting my own government for 12 years.

Three weeks after the Bin Laden mission, we go to Leon Panetta’s retirement ceremony in Langley, Virginia. He gets off stage and literally brings over Hollywood producers and directors, saying, ‘Hey look, they’re going to make you famous.’ They had full White House and CIA access to make Zero Dark Thirty.

I was an enlisted guy. I’m sitting there watching every single politician and leader from Washington talk about their heroic decisions for reelection campaigns, while none of the 24 operators who actually kicked the doors got any credit.

When I wrote No Easy Day, the government immediately came after me with unlimited attorneys. In the end, they admitted there was nothing classified in the book—they just wanted all the money back.

I spent $1.5 million of that money defending myself against their accusations. The government said, ‘We want that back too.’

So they put me on a garnishment plan: $3,800 every single month for the next 15 years. They told me if I miss one payment, they’ll charge me back taxes and prosecute me again.

I served this country for 14 straight combat tours. When I got out, I received a plaque with my first name misspelled—one ‘T’ in Matt. And now they want me paying them back for longer than I even wore the uniform.”

Washington politicians and intelligence officials handed classified access to Hollywood filmmakers for Zero Dark Thirty, yet when an enlisted SEAL who kicked the doors in Abbottabad wrote about his own experience, the federal government stripped every penny he earned and put him on a 15-year garnishment plan.

Is this one of the most disgraceful double standards in military history? Drop your thoughts below.

For the first time in its 100-year history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed off Thanksgiving Day due to severe weather (Axios, KTVU).

Organizers announced on Wednesday that the 100th march will move to Saturday, November 28, stepping off at 8.30 a.m. ET as a powerful nor'easter threatens New York City with heavy rain and high winds (TheWrap, CBS News New York).

Under New York City safety rules, the parade's giant helium balloons cannot fly if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts top 34 mph, and Thursday's High Wind Warning called for gusts up to 48 to 60 mph across the metro area (Nacionale, FOX 5 New York).

Will you still tune in on Saturday morning, or does it just not feel the same outside Thanksgiving Day?

$1 MILLION MASSACHUSETTS LOTTERY WINNER ARRESTED BY ICE IN BOSTON DAYS AFTER POSING WITH HIS JACKPOT CHECKDESPITE HAVING A FEDERAL DEPORTATION ORDER SINCE 2014

An East Boston man who posed smiling with a giant $1 million Massachusetts State Lottery check last week is now in federal immigration custody after ICE Boston arrested him on Tuesday (ICE, CTV News).

On November 18, lottery officials announced that Ariel Velasquez won $1 million on a "$2,000,000 50X Cashword" scratch ticket purchased in East Boston, taking the $650,000 one-time pre-tax cash payout (CTV News).

Just six days later, ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations in Boston arrested Ariel Velasquez-Morales, stating he is a Salvadoran national who entered the United States illegally in May 2013 and was ordered deported by an immigration judge in April 2014 (ICE, CTV News).

Should state lotteries run federal warrant or deportation checks before handing out major jackpot payouts, or should prize claims stay strictly separate from immigration enforcement?

The U.S. Army has issued a new request for proposals offering land at nine military installations—including Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and Fort Hood, Texas—for 25-year leases to build commercial power plants and AI data centers (MLQ.ai, Beveridge & Diamond).

Under the November 20 solicitation, data-center-only bids are excluded, and selected projects must be able to supply backup power to the base within one hour of a grid outage for at least 14 continuous days (MLQ.ai).

At the same time, veteran advocacy group Veterans for Public Lands has called for an immediate pause on new data center development on federal public lands (Reddit / Military.com).

Should private AI data centers be built on U.S. military bases in exchange for backup power, or should federal land stay off limits?

A U.S. Border Patrol agent on horseback galloped down a mountain trail near El Paso after CBP air support spotted an illegal immigrant hiding in the brush on a steep ridge.

Working together from the air and on horseback, CBP agents talked the mounted officer straight to the hiding spot to complete the arrest in rugged terrain.

How effective are mounted horse units paired with air support along the southern border?

After the House voted 211–204 on November 10 to refer his eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) is shifting his focus toward forcing a House floor vote to pull U.S. troops out of the Iran war (CBS News, Just Security).

Massie introduced H. Con. Res. 126 under Section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to direct the removal of U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran without congressional authorization (GovInfo, Arab Center Washington DC). In recent interviews, Massie called a new War Powers vote a "lifeboat" for Republicans following the party's midterm losses (Newsweek, The Hill).

Hegseth and President Donald Trump have defended the military operations against Iran as lawful and necessary, with Hegseth dismissing Massie's impeachment push as a "farce" and "political spectacle" (CBS News).

Should Congress vote to withdraw U.S. forces from the Iran conflict, or leave operational decisions to the White House and Pentagon?

#ThomasMassie #PeteHegseth

In September 2003, on her 3rd day in Iraq, Captain Kellie McCoy commanded a company from the 307th Engineers Battalion, 82nd Airborne. McCoy and 10 other soldiers set off on a convoy of 4 vehicles near Fallujah when they were ambushed with IEDs, automatic weapons, and RPGs. McCoy's humvee escaped serious damage, but the other 3 vehicles were disabled by the daisy-chain explosions. McCoy exited her vehicle and directed her soldiers toward her humvee. She returned fire at the ambushers, shooting two insurgents firing an RPG at the convoy. Most of her ammo was gone by the time she piled all 11 combat-loaded soldiers into her humvee and exited the kill zone. They returned to base with minor injuries, and no one was killed. For her outstanding role in directing the response of her column to the ambush and helping ensure everyone made it back alive, McCoy was awarded a Bronze Star with "V".
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
McCoy retired from the Army as a Lieutenant Colonel after 20 years of service. During that time, she served 3 tours in Iraq and 1 in Afghanistan. She is now the founder and CEO of her own company.

Microsoft has declared an internal "Code Red" inside its Microsoft 365 division after a historic 24-hour global outage on November 12–13 knocked out Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, according to internal memos obtained by Reuters (CTV News).

M365 Core President Jason Henderson told staff that "Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team" and admitted "Never before had so many customers been without email for so long" (MLQ.ai). Corporate VP Amanda Silver wrote that engineers worked through a "fog of war," trading more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats as they scrambled to restore service (Seeking Alpha).

Microsoft blamed the disruption on an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, ruled out cyberattacks or AI agents, and set a new target of deploying urgent fixes globally within one hour (The Next Web, Investing.com).

Did the November outage hit your workplace or email, and do you trust cloud providers to hit a one-hour recovery goal?

Trump stopped the turkey pardon to thank the troops guarding Hormuz.

Main post (the “read”):
During the annual White House Thanksgiving turkey ceremony on November 24, President Trump paused the lighthearted tradition to speak directly about the service members enforcing the naval presence in the Strait of Hormuz.

He thanked the troops standing watch and asked God to watch over and protect all of the military.

While the rest of the country gets ready for holiday tables, those sailors and service members are still on station in one of the most strategically critical waterways in the world.

It’s a small moment in a long ceremony, but it puts the focus where it belongs this week.

If you’re thankful for them today, say so in the comments.

Live footage captured plumes of smoke rising near Middletown, lowa, around 9 a.m. CT on Wednesday as the U.S. Army carried out a controlled detonation of roughly 5 tons of unstable lead azide (FOX 9, The Guardian).
Residents within 5 miles of the lowa Army Ammunition Plant were told to evacuate, while FEMA advised everyone within 20 miles
-including Middletown, Augusta, and Burlington-to shelter indoors with windows closed to avoid airborne lead dust (FOX 9).
The Army said it installed blast barriers, ballistic gels, foams, and water mitigation ahead of the blast, and the EPA collected more than 1,200 air, land, and water samples to measure lead levels before and after the operation (The Guardian, PBS NewsHour).

Do you think the Army handled this controlled detonation safely, or should it have waited longer?
This was sent out around 10 minutes ago (screenshot sent to me by a person who lives close to the explosion location)

Would you back former White House aide John McEntee or Secretary of State Marco Rubio in 2028?

According to Emerson College Polling, Marco Rubio recently led a national 2028 Republican nomination poll with 44% support, ahead of Vice President JD Vance at 24%, though Rubio has publicly stated he has no current plans to run (CNN). Supporters of Rubio point to his Senate and State Department foreign-policy experience, while observers cited by i24NEWS note he faces questions over how closely his record is tied to the current administration.

Meanwhile, Axios and IBTimes UK report that former White House Presidential Personnel Office Director John McEntee now a conservative TikTok creator with over 3.3 million followers has topped recent College Republican 2028 straw polls at Notre Dame, Penn State, and the University of Tennessee. Supporters highlight his grassroots digital reach and loyalty to President Trump, while critics point to his 2018 security-clearance dismissal and his registered lobbying work for Chinese technology firms (Wikipedia).

Where do you stand on a hypothetical 2028 matchup between McEntee and Rubio?

#Election2028 #JohnMcEntee #MarcoRubio

Gunnery Sgt. Aubrey McDade
1st Battalion, 8th Marines
Fallujah, Iraq, Nov. 11, 2004
Award: Navy Cross

Shortly after departing their base in Fallujah, then-Sgt. McDade and 1/8 Bravo Company's 1st Platoon entered an alley and encountered an immediate heavy volume of small arms and machine gun fire. In the opening seconds of the engagement, three Marines were seriously wounded as the well positioned and expecting enemy pinned others down. On contact, McDade rushed from the rear of the platoon column toward the kill zone and immediately deployed a machine gun team into the alley to provide suppressive fire on the enemy. After several attempts to reach casualties in the alley were met with heavy, well-aimed machine gun fire, he showed total disregard for his own safety by moving across the alley and successfully extracting the first of three wounded Marines from the kill zone. Aware of the fact that there were still two wounded Marines in the alley, McDade dashed through the heart of the kill zone two more times, each time braving intense enemy fire to successfully retrieve a Marine. After extracting the last casualty from the kill zone, he assisted in their treatment and medical evacuation. His quick thinking and aggressive actions were crucial in saving the lives of two of the three casualties.

“My son who followed his great grandfather's footsteps, my late grandfather Duley Bonito who was a Marine, fought in the Korean war. He joined the Marine Corps and is now officially our "Apache" U.S Marine of the W.M.A.T as well.

We are all so very happy and proud of him! He was happy to see us there and I wouldn't miss it for the world!” -S. S. 

#usmcfamily #usmc

Sgt. 1st Class Christopher Celiz 🇺🇸

On July 12, 2018, in Afghanistan, Sgt. 1st Class Celiz gave his life to protect his team and save an Afghan partner. Wounded by enemy fire, he used his body to shield others and called for evacuation, putting his brothers before himself to the very end.

For his valor, he was awarded the Medal of Honor.

We will never forget his courage and sacrifice. Please take a moment to honor him below. 🙏

#GiftOfValor #NeverForget #MedalOfHonor

Today we honor Sgt. Rafael Peralta 🇺🇸

On November 15, 2004, in Fallujah, Iraq, Sgt. Peralta gave his life to save his fellow Marines. During house-to-house clearing, he was wounded by gunfire, yet when an enemy grenade landed near his team, he pulled it to his body to shield his brothers from the blast.

For his valor, he was awarded the Navy Cross.

We will never forget his courage and sacrifice. Please take a moment to honor him below. 🙏

#GiftOfValor #NeverForget #NavyCross

“WE WERE EIGHT GUYS ON A ROOFTOP SURROUNDED BY THOUSANDS OF MILITIA FIRING THOUSANDS OF ROUNDS A MINUTE.”

On April 4, 2004, the holy city of Najaf, Iraq erupted into chaos as Muqtada al-Sadr’s Mahdi Army launched a coordinated uprising against coalition forces.

At the Coalition Provisional Authority (CPA) compound, a small detachment of eight Blackwater security contractors including former U.S. Marine Force Recon sniper Travis Haley found themselves cut off, outnumbered, and fighting for their lives against an advancing force of thousands.

Sitting down on The Shawn Ryan Show (SRS #172), Haley broke down the unvarnished reality of the legendary rooftop siege:

“The Mahdi Army had completely encircled the compound. We were on the roof eight guys with small arms and precision rifles looking out at hundreds, if not thousands, of armed insurgents advancing down the streets. You could literally hear the roar of the crowd before the firing started. When they opened up, the air filled with RPGs, mortars, and PKM rounds chewing up the parapet walls.”

“Brass was piling up past our ankles. I was on my precision rifle engaging targets one after another, working the bolt so fast that the barrel was smoking. At one point, I looked over at the guys next to me. We were out of ammunition resupplies, Spanish military forces inside had barricaded themselves below, and we knew if they breached the courtyard walls, we were going to be lynched and burned.”

“In that moment, fear disappears. You stop worrying about dying, lock your focus down to your optic, and decide that every single round left in your mags is taking an enemy down with you.”

Key takeaways from Haley’s breakdown of the battle:

The eight-man team manned the rooftop parapets for hours under non-stop direct fire, repelling wave after wave of militia assaults attempting to breach the perimeter gates.

With ammunition virtually exhausted and coalition ground reinforcements blocked, civilian Blackwater helicopter pilots braved intense anti-aircraft fire to hover directly over the embattled roof and kick out crates of 5.56mm and 7.62mm ammo.

The Warrior Mindset Under Siege: When survival looks impossible, combat psychology shifts from panic to cold, lethal execution—focusing strictly on fundamentals and making every pull of the trigger count.

The iconic footage of Haley working his precision rifle on that Najaf rooftop became one of the most widely watched combat videos of the early Iraq War.

Have you listened to Travis Haley’s full breakdown on SRS #172 yet?

On the morning of September 11, 2001, 34-year-old FDNY firefighter Stephen Siller had just completed a long shift with Brooklyn’s elite Squad 1 and was driving home to meet his brothers for a round of golf. When his emergency scanner announced that an airliner had struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center, Siller immediately turned his vehicle around and headed straight toward Manhattan.

Arriving at the entrance of the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, Siller found it already barricaded and closed to all vehicular traffic for emergency security. Knowing his brother firefighters were already rushing into the burning towers across the river, Siller refused to turn back.

He strapped sixty pounds of heavy firefighting turnout gear onto his back, abandoned his vehicle at the entrance, and began sprinting on foot through nearly two miles of gridlocked subterranean darkness toward the financial district.

Emerging into lower Manhattan, Siller raced directly to the World Trade Center and entered the towers alongside fellow first responders to help evacuate thousands of civilians trapped on the upper floors. Siller gave his life that morning when the towers collapsed, leaving behind his wife and five young children. His legendary determination inspired his family to establish the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, an organization that has since provided debt-free homes and support to thousands of fallen first responder families, catastrophically injured service members, and Gold Star families nationwide.

What does Stephen Siller’s two-mile sprint through the darkness teach us about the true heart of a firefighter?

#StephenSiller #TunnelToTowers #FDNY

This is the Iowa "lead fallout" map circulating across social media ahead of tomorrow's 9 a.m. controlled detonation but should people actually be worried? (PBS News)

The U.S. Army is set to detonate 68 barrels roughly 5 tons of unstable, conventional lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, after the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected an emergency halt (Quartz, Al Jazeera). While the viral graphic shades more than 20 eastern states, official Army emergency alerts cover 5 to 20 miles southwest toward Missouri, and even Earthjustice's lawsuit warning cited a potential plume of at least 100 miles depending on winds (CBS News Chicago, Earthjustice).

Do you think the Army's containment safeguards are enough, or are nearby residents right to be concerned?

"It's your responsibility, as a protector, to become better at violence than evil men."

Being peaceful isn't the same as being harmless. Real readiness comes from discipline, training, and the willingness to step up and protect the people you love before trouble ever knocks.

Save this as a reminder to stay sharp, stay disciplined, and keep training.

#ProtectorMindset #Preparedness #SelfDefense

With his scheduled December 3 firing-squad execution just days away, convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan has asked a federal court for a stay so he can prepare a habeas corpus petition challenging his sentence (AP News, CBS News).

The former U.S. Army psychiatrist was convicted in 2013 and sentenced to death for murdering 13 people and wounding 32 others in the November 2009 attack at Fort Hood, Texas (U.S. Army).

ACLU attorneys acting as standby counsel urged the court on Tuesday to pause the execution to allow federal habeas review (ACLU). If carried out as scheduled, it would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961 and the first by firing squad since 1945 (Death Penalty Info Center).

Should the federal court grant a last-minute stay or let the December 3 execution move forward?

Today we honor Staff Sgt. Robert J. Miller 🇺🇸

On January 25, 2008, in Afghanistan, Staff Sgt. Miller gave his life to save his team. When his patrol was ambushed, he charged directly into enemy fire to draw attention away from his brothers, allowing them to move to safety.

For his valor, he was awarded the Medal of Honor.

We will never forget his courage and sacrifice. Please take a moment to honor him below. 🙏

#GiftOfValor #NeverForget #MedalOfHonor

Erik Prince Analyzes The Butler Security Failure On The Shawn Ryan Show
Shawn Ryan Show Appearance Former Navy SEAL officer and Blackwater founder Erik Prince joined The Shawn Ryan Show Episode 123 for a technical tactical breakdown of the catastrophic security collapse during the July 13, 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania

In Erik Prince’s Own Words

“I spent decades running high-threat protection details for ambassadors, CIA directors, and heads of state in places like Baghdad, Kabul, and Fallujah. In protective security, rule number one is dominating the high ground inside the direct line-of-sight weapon range. An AGR building 130 yards away from the principal with an unobstructed sightline is target number one on any site survey. Any rookie detail leader secures that roof hours before the protectee ever steps on stage. Instead, you had local law enforcement warning them, citizens on the street filming a guy crawling onto the roof with a rifle for several minutes, and leadership failing to act. To leave a direct line-of-sight roof 130 yards away open, without a single counter-sniper team physically occupying it, defies every standard operating procedure in protective security history. That isn’t an innocent oversight—it is either catastrophic negligence or institutional corruption.”

After waiting 25 years to put on the uniform and spending 13 months securing multiple age and dependent waivers Christopher Harper arrived at Navy Recruit Training Command in Great Lakes, Illinois, three months after his 42nd birthday and graduated at the top of his class (Task & Purpose).

During a division fitness challenge to earn a phone call home after six weeks without speaking to his family, Harper ran a 10-minute 1.5-mile run, knocked out 112 push-ups, and held a 12-minute plank, earning the Military Excellence Award.

Now training at Corry Station in Pensacola, Florida, to become a cryptologic technician, he says he's considering a commission and hopes to serve 20 years.

Drop a salute in the comments for proving it's never too late to chase a dream.

#USNavy #NavyBootCamp

🚨BREAKING NEWS 🚨The Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some unclassified information, according to The New York Times, Reuters, and the Associated Press (CTV News, Jerusalem Post).

An AP source confirmed that an unclassified CIA system was compromised in a cyberattack (KTAR). The disclosure comes just days after separate reports that the FBI's National Crime Information Center database was also targeted in an apparent intrusion (KREM).

How concerned are you about back-to-back cyber intrusions hitting U.S. intelligence and law-enforcement agencies?

The first public look at the surface-launched variant of the "Rusty Dagger" low-cost cruise missile just broke cover as manufacturer Zone 5 Technologies dramatically expands nationwide production to prepare for high-end conflict in the Pacific, according to reporting from The War Zone.

Originally developed under the U.S. Air Force's Extended Range Attack Munition (ERAM) program as the air-launched AGM-188A—which has already seen operational combat service in Ukraine—the weapon is now being adapted for ground-based containerized launchers. To meet surging Pentagon demand, Zone 5 is expanding manufacturing facilities across California, Texas, and Ohio, scaling toward a combined annual capacity of over 7,500 missiles by late 2027.

The ground-launched missile directly feeds into the Air Force's Family of Affordable Mass Missiles (FAMM) initiative, which seeks to acquire 28,000 low-cost standoff weapons over the next five years. Operating from dispersed island outposts and mobile trailers across the first island chain, these mass-produced cruise missiles give ground forces the ability to launch saturation strikes against adversary warship formations without needing to risk multi-million-dollar aircraft or surface combatants.

Will affordable mass-produced cruise missiles be the ultimate equalizer against China's naval shipbuilding numbers in the Pacific? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.

Joe Kent Relives The Moment He Learned Of Shannon Kent’s Sacrifice In Syria
Shawn Ryan Show Appearance Former Green Beret, CIA operative, and Gold Star husband Joe Kent joined The Shawn Ryan Show Episode 126 to recount his military career, family life, and the devastating morning notification following the death of his wife

The Manbij Suicide Attack Navy Senior Chief Cryptologic Technician Shannon M. Kent, operating alongside special operations units with the Intelligence Support Activity, was killed on January 16, 2019, when an ISIS suicide bomber detonated an explosive vest at a restaurant in Manbij, Syria

In Joe Kent’s Own Words

“I had retired from special operations to stay home and raise our two toddler boys while Shannon deployed to northern Syria to hunt ISIS networks. It was early morning, around 6:00 a.m. I was in the kitchen making breakfast for our boys when I heard the knock. You spend 20 years in the military knowing what that knock means. I walked to the front door, looked through the window, and saw two officers standing on my front porch in dress blues. Your stomach drops through the floorboards. Your entire reality shatters before the door even opens. They said, ‘Mr. Kent, we regret to inform you that Senior Chief Shannon Kent was killed in action in Manbij.’ An ISIS suicide bomber walked into a restaurant where our team was meeting with local leaders and detonated a vest. In a flash, my wife was gone, and our boys were left without their mother. That was the moment my life pivoted toward demanding accountability for the decisions that put our troops in harm's way.”

The Navy’s newest carrier class finally landed an F-35C.

Main post (the “read”):
In October 2026, the future USS John F. Kennedy completed the first F-35C launch and recovery trials on a Ford-class aircraft carrier.

Two jets flew 34 sorties and logged 122 catapult launches and 122 arrested landings using the ship’s Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System and Advanced Arresting Gear.

This was a long time coming.

The lead ship, USS Gerald R. Ford, has operated for years without the F-35C in its air wing, largely due to design and integration challenges with the new systems. It has continued flying Super Hornets while the Navy worked through the issues.

Now the second ship in the class has proven the stealth fighter can operate from the Ford-class deck.

It’s a quiet but important milestone for both the carrier and the F-35C program.

Why did it take so long?
That’s the question a lot of people are still asking.

Former NYPD officer and fired New York City public school teacher's aide Sayed Mohassib, 27, confessed in a published jailhouse interview on November 21 to fatally stabbing 28-year-old Brooklyn jogger Katie Suarez—claiming "Allah told me to kill a person" (Hindustan Times, South Shore Press).

Suarez, an avid marathon runner and bank teller, was stabbed in the neck while jogging along Brooklyn's Shore Parkway Greenway on October 30 and died three days later (CNN, FOX 5 New York). Although Mohassib initially pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder, tampering with evidence, and weapon possession, the case has also triggered outrage over how he was hired at P.S. 200 in Brooklyn after leaving the NYPD in 2022 and being rejected in 2023 following concerning behavior and a psychiatric evaluation (FOX 5 New York, CNN).

NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Department of Education have terminated Mohassib and ordered a full review of school hiring and screening practices (FOX 5 New York). How did someone flagged during a police psych screening end up working inside an elementary school?
I really want this!

Do you still trust Secretary of War Pete Hegseth?

A former top aide is now calling for him to resign.

Joe Kasper, who served as Hegseth’s original chief of staff, said his former boss has lost the ability to be effective. He criticized the handling of the Iran conflict, the relationship with Congress, and what he described as an overindulgence in ego over the institution.

At the same time, supporters continue to defend Hegseth’s aggressive overhaul of the Pentagon — the firings, the cultural changes, and the push to reshape the military’s leadership.

The divide is clear.
One side sees a necessary disruption of a bloated system.
The other sees a leadership style that has burned too many bridges and left the department weaker.

The question is landing harder than usual right now.

Do you still trust him?

Stephen Edward Austin
DATE OF BIRTH: June 1, 1947

CITATION:
The President of the United States of America takes pride in presenting the Navy Cross (Posthumously) to Corporal Stephen Edward Austin (MCSN: 2127411), United States Marine Corps, for extraordinary heroism in action against the enemy while serving as a Squad Leader with Company C, First Battalion, Twenty-Seventh Marine Regiment, FIRST Marine Division, in the Republic of Vietnam on 8 June 1968. While on a combat patrol approaching the village of Cu Ban 4, Corporal Austin's platoon was taken under enemy fire from a nearby bunker, immediately killing or wounding several Marines. Determined to silence the bunker and retrieve his fallen comrades, Corporal Austin convinced his platoon leader not to fall back and call in an air strike. Corporal Austin brilliantly maneuvered his squad to an area from which they could provide effective covering fire on the enemy bunker. With complete disregard for his own safety, Corporal Austin single-handedly assaulted the bunker and destroyed it with a grenade. Although mortally wounded in the attack, he was successful in turning the tide of the engagement, which led to the complete elimination of the enemy within the village. Corporal Austin's bold action, courage under fire, and complete dedication to duty reflected great credit upon him and were in keeping with the highest traditions of the military service and reflect great credit upon himself, the Marine Corps, and the United States Naval Service.

Hospitality businesses across the country have been caught in the crossfire of immigration enforcement throughout 2026. Earlier this year, an Arizona Mexican restaurant owner immigrant from El Salvador faced waves of angry calls alongside supportive customers after confirming his standing policy of free meals for law enforcement also applied to federal ICE agents (Newsmax, WFMD).

On the other side, restaurant operators in cities like Minneapolis and Chicago joined strikes, criticized enforcement surges for hurting local foot traffic, or refused service to ICE agents (The Guardian, Restaurant Business Online).

Supporters of free-meal policies view them as routine appreciation for law enforcement officers, while critics argue businesses should not subsidize or normalize federal immigration raids. Would you support a local restaurant that offers free food to ICE agents? Sound off below.

Early 1990s. Fort Bragg flat range.

A 1st SFOD-D (Delta Force) operator running high-speed, live-fire pistol drills around steel barrels.

The loadout is pure perfection:

Silkies

White sneakers

Black ball cap & dark shades

Thigh-rig drop-leg holster

Custom combat pistol

An absolute unit of a 90s tactical mustache

Long before the internet era of $1,000 designer combat pants, high-cut carbon helmets, and tactical Instagram influencers, Tier-1 marksmanship was built on one thing: relentless, blistering repetition.

Delta assaulters spent countless hours burning through tens of thousands of rounds of ammunition on the flat range until drawing, driving the gun, and putting double-taps on target at point-blank speed became pure, subconscious instinct.

No plate carrier. No tactical fashion. Just peak physical conditioning, speed, and pure lethality.

Modern gear is great, but fundamentals never go out of style.

Drop a 🇺🇸 below to honor the golden era of Delta Force. Peak performance in the flesh.

America’s stealth destroyers are getting hypersonic missiles.

All three Zumwalt-class destroyers are being converted to carry Conventional Prompt Strike missiles.

These are hypersonic weapons — traveling at Mach 5 or faster — designed for rapid, long-range conventional strikes.

Each ship will carry 12 of them.

The Navy is removing the original large guns that never fully delivered and replacing that space with vertical launch tubes for these new missiles.

The Zumwalts were once criticized as expensive ships searching for a mission.
Now they’re being turned into the first surface ships in the U.S. fleet armed with operational hypersonic strike capability.

Supporters say this finally gives the class a clear, high-end role in peer competition.
Critics still question the cost, the limited numbers, and whether three ships with 12 missiles each will move the needle enough.

Game changer… or expensive niche capability?

The FBI has arrested 37-year-old Leonard Michael Fierro of Hacienda Heights, California, on a federal criminal complaint charging him with one count of interstate threats against ICE officers, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

Federal prosecutors allege investigators recovered videos in which Fierro discussed initiating a violent revolution, targeting ICE agents, and encouraging armed attacks on government facilities (DOJ Central District of California, NewsNation). According to the complaint, agents also found a farewell video in which Fierro stated he expected to be found "riddled with bullet holes," alongside notes with Spanish-language phrases intended for communicating with detainees during a planned effort to free individuals from an ICE detention facility (DOJ Central District of California).

Fierro—arrested Friday with assistance from the Federal Protective Service, Homeland Security Investigations, and the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department—faces a statutory maximum of five years in federal prison if convicted (DOJ Central District of California).

Would you support a Sharia ban in your state’s courts?

Alabama and Tennessee have passed laws barring judges from applying foreign or religious law including Sharia when it conflicts with constitutional rights.

Supporters say the laws put the U.S. legal system first. Critics, including the Brennan Center for Justice, argue they target Muslims, while some legal scholars say they address a problem that doesn’t exist.

Should your state adopt a similar ban, or keep the law as it is?

NYC Mayor proposes $500 a month to families housing former inmates.

As part of his 88-page plan to close Rikers Island, Mayor Zohran Mamdani is expanding a program that pays families to house relatives returning from jail or prison.

The Kinship Reentry Housing Program currently supports about 50 families.
The new plan would grow that to 300.

Right now, participating households receive $500 a month for up to 12 months to help cover the cost of taking someone in.

The goal is to give people leaving incarceration a stable place to land instead of cycling back into the system or ending up on the street.

Supporters say family housing can reduce recidivism and ease pressure on the city’s jail population as Rikers is phased out.
Critics argue it’s another use of taxpayer money that rewards the wrong incentives.

On March 23, 2003, Captain Allen Grinalds flew his Cobra attack helicopter over Iraq back home towards Kuwait. He had been in the air for 10 hours supporting Marines on the way to Baghdad. A call for help came through from British troops under an artillery barrage near Basra. Despite being low on fuel and exhausted, Grinalds and 3 pilots with him knew they were the only ones close enough to help. As they neared the city, anti-aircraft fire came up in a wall, forcing Grinalds to turn back. He came in from another direction, so low the Iraqi gunners could not depress their guns enough to fire at them. The Marine pilots found the artillery pieces pummeling the British and opened up. As he neared, Grinalds noticed several Iraqi tanks preparing to move on the British. Before the tanks could turn anything on his helicopters, Grinalds fired rockets, lighting two of them up. Mayhem spread through the enemy on the ground as the helicopters chewed through them. Artillery pieces, tanks, and anti-aircraft guns exploded as the Cobras expended every single rocket and round they had. Grinalds finally left the battlefield running on fumes, making it 8 miles back to base.

For his role leading the rescue mission and skillful initiative in thwarting the Iraqi force, Grinalds was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross. Nearly a decade later, He was awarded the Bronze Star while a Lieutenant Colonel serving as CO of HMLA-269 during their deployment in Afghanistan. He retired from the Marines after 20 years of service.

Lance Corporal Joshua Moore occupied a hide near Marjah, Afghanistan, with several other scout snipers when their position came under attack. Two Marines right outside the structure fell wounded. Suddenly, Moore felt something bounce off his back. He turned and found two enemy grenades on the floor. Without hesitation, Moore picked up one and threw it out the door, where the grenade safely exploded away from the Marines. As he grabbed the second grenade to throw back, he realized it was corroded and defective. Moore then ran outside into the enemy fire to help the wounded. Using his M4 and grenade launcher, Moore neutralized the enemy position 100 meters away while others moved the casualties to safety. Moore then helped clear a LZ for medevac.

For his heroic actions, at risk to his own life, two years later Moore was awarded the Navy Cross. He had been promoted to Sergeant by the time of the award.

“...serving with Scout Sniper Platoon, Second Battalion, Eighth Marines, on 14 March 2011 in support of Operation ENDURING FREEDOM. LCpl Moore demonstrated audacity and selfless devotion to duty in the face of a determined enemy when his element came under attack north of Marjah. Two Marines who were outside the structure the team was using for cover immediately became casualties. Insurgents then threw two grenades over the wall into the team's position. Without hesitation and with complete disregard for his own life, LCpl Moore picked up the first grenade and threw it out of the building, where it immediately detonated. He then picked up the second grenade, recognized it had malfunctioned and would not detonate, discarded it, and charged out of the structure to aid the wounded. Though instantly taken under fire by an enemy force one hundred meters away, LCpl Moore stood his ground, returning fire with his M-4 rifle and M-203 grenade launcher. The effects of his fire neutralized the enemy and forced them to abandon their position, buying his team time to regroup and aid their wounded. He then immediately took action to assist in securing a landing zone to extract wounded personnel.”

“If you took 100 Doug Zembiecs to war with you, you could conquer the world.” That is how Maj. Zembiec’s high-school wrestling coach characterized him – though the men who served with him captured his spirit more succinctly: He was reverently called the “Lion of Fallujah.” A magnetic commander, an “unapologetic warrior,” Zembiec believed in leading by deeds rather than words. As a result, his men would tell you that they would follow Zembiec to the gates of hell – or, at the very least, into the treacherous urban battlefield of Fallujah.

In early April of 2004, Zembiec’s company was sent in to help pacify Fallujah and restore order in a city where violence had spiraled out of control. During the month-long battle to claim Fallujah, Zembiec’s Echo Company was often the first one in and the last one out.

On April 6, Zembiec, a captain at the time, found himself deep in insurgent territory in Fallujah’s Jolan district.

A Marine patrol was taking heavy fire, and Zembiec’s unit was called in to lead a retaliatory assault. Right after arriving, Echo Company rushed toward the enemies, who launched a heavy volley of fire toward the new arrivals. Instead of directing from the back, Zembiec himself led the men toward the fire, determined to help the trapped patrol.

His men moved to a roof to counter the insurgents who had been firing down from above. The enemies wasted no time and focused their AK-47- and RPG-fire on the Marines on the roof. The Marines tried to radio an Abrams tank to fire on the enemy, but the tank didn’t respond. As they continued to call for assistance, Zembiec decided to take matters into his own hands.

He raced down the stairs and directly into the line of fire, heading toward the tank. He climbed up to the hatch even as mortar rounds exploded nearby and bullets ricocheted off the metal. Unscathed, he told the tank operators where to fire. The tank made quick work of the enemy, and Zembiec ran back to the roof. Witnesses say the other Marines dropped their jaws in awe of his bravery.

A few weeks later, on April 26, insurgents opened fire on Zembiec’s platoon from three sides, with thousands of rounds. Grenades flew back and forth between the enemy and his men – with only 20 feet between them. Zembiec, wounded by shrapnel, moved to a better position to direct the counterattack. He then moved from house to house, encouraging and motivating his men and repositioning the outnumbered Marines. Even as the battle raged, Zembiec coordinated the evacuation of nine injured Marines.

Later, despite being assigned to a desk job, Zembiec volunteered to return to the frontlines. He completed a tour in Afghanistan and returned to Iraq again. On May 11, 2007, Zembiec was killed in Baghdad, Iraq, while leading a combat operation.

When people think of warriors and heroes, images of legendary Spartans or Trojans often come to mind. The tales of those warriors may have faded into history, but that same timeless courage and heroism lives on in a new breed of heroes – men like Doug Zembiec, the “Lion of Fallujah.”

For his month-long fight in Fallujah, Zembiec received a Bronze Star for Valor on Dec. 9, 2004.

Army Col. Robert L. Howard, 70, of San Antonio. TX. passed away on December 23, 2009. He served with 5th Special Forces Group (Airborne), 1st Special Forces, Military Assistance Command, Vietnam-Studies and Observation Group. Col Howard received the Medal of Honor for his actions while serving in Vietnam.

The #MedalofHonor is the highest military decoration awarded by the United States government to service members who distinguish themselves through gallantry and intrepidity, risking his or her life above and beyond the call of duty against enemies of the United States of America.

Colonel Howard was awarded his medal for his actions in #Vietnam. As a sergeant first class, he served as a platoon sergeant of an American-Vietnamese platoon. The platoon was attacked by an estimated two-company force. Although he was wounded and unable to walk, he crawled through heavy gunfire to retrieve his wounded leader and rejoin the platoon. He rallied the platoon into an organized defensive force, administered first aid and directed the defenders to repulse enemy attacks for three and a half hours.

“CH-53K REFUELS IN MID-AIR WHILE SLING-LOADING AN F-35C STEALTH JET OFF THE COAST OF NEW JERSEY.”

In one of the most remarkable aviation feats in modern military history, a U.S. Marine Corps CH-53K King Stallion heavy-lift helicopter conducted an in-flight aerial refueling from a KC-130 Hercules while externally slinging a 22,000-pound F-35C Lightning II airframe over the Atlantic Ocean.

Piloted by Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron One (VMX-1) in coordination with the F-35 Integrated Test Force, the mission transported the carrier-variant stealth jet airframe from NAS Patuxent River, Maryland, to Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst, New Jersey:

Unmatched Heavy-Lift Power: Powered by three General Electric T408 turboshaft engines producing 22,500 total horsepower, the CH-53K can carry an external payload of up to 36,000 pounds—nearly triple the lift capability of its predecessor in hot-and-high conditions.

Mid-Air Refueling Under Load: Connecting to the KC-130's refueling drogue with a 22,000-pound fighter suspended by steel cables required precision flight control, fly-by-wire stability, and steady rotor aerodynamics over open water.

Expeditionary Recovery (TRAP): The demonstration validated that the Marine Corps can execute long-range Tactical Recovery of Aircraft and Personnel (TRAP) for fifth-generation fighters across contested island chains and remote expeditionary advanced bases.

Infinite Operational Range: Combining heavy external sling capabilities with aerial refueling allows the King Stallion to transport heavy artillery, armored combat vehicles, and damaged aircraft across vast maritime distances without stopping.

American aerospace engineering operating at the absolute limit.
